newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy debt/GDP ratio a market risk factor - Draghi.
newsitem.headline: Italy debt/GDP ratio a market risk factor - Draghi.

text.p: Italy will remain fragile in the view of financial markets until the country gets round to overhauling its bloated public debt and state accounts, Treasury director-general Mario Draghi said.

"Italy is suffering from fragility linked to the state debt/gross domestic product ratio and this will expose it to market turbulence until the ratio is corrected," Draghi said at the presentation of a Banca Commerciale Italiana newsletter.

Italy has a debt mountain of around 2,000 trillion lire ($1.2 trillion), estimated at above 122 percent of GDP this year, over double the 60 percent Maastricht target for the single European currency.
EU Commissioner Mario Monti warned Italy on Monday of the dangers of being swept away by euphoria as stock and bond prices soared to all-time highs on hopes Italy will join a European currency union.
"Since the end of 1996 Italy has made big progress but beware of being blinded by euphoria," Monti told Rome daily La Repubblica in an interview.

The government is engaged in a do or die bid to slash a large public sector deficit -- the biggest single obstacle to Italy being admitted to European economic and monetary union (EMU) -- and financial markets are applauding.

But Monti said that with Germany and France experiencing difficulties with the 3.0 percent deficit/GDP goal, there were signs the spotlight was being shifted on to the public debt question, "and in particular on Italy."
Italy therefore had to implement "serious and rapid action on structural reforms...starting with pensions," Monti said.
Talks between the government, trades unions and employers on the thorny issue of pension reform are due to begin on Tuesday.
Draghi said the crucial talks on streamlining Italy's welfare state should lead to a lightening of the weight of social contributions in order to boost jobs and growth.

Welfare state reform "should provide a definitive response to the need to review mechanisms forming the base of the dynamics of current expenditure and could furthermore provide an opportunity to marry stability and growth," Draghi said.

He noted that the level of social contributions in Italy was the highest among G7 nations. "It is a heavy tax on employment and so reduces the number of those who could contribute to the funding of the pensions system."

He said he hoped eventual reforms would produce "innovative and substantial results, bringing avout benefits to public finances such as to allow on one hand an increase in social spending where it is lacking and on the other hand to reduce the weight of contributions."
"This would trigger a virtuous circle where the lower weight of contributions would encourage growth and employment," he added.
